extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO officials, legislators, policy stakeholders, and affected industry (e.g., banks, inventors)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and implementation guidance for major provisions of S.23/The America Invents Act, including post-grant review, the Schumer-Kyl transitional business-method proceeding, first-inventor-to-file rules, venue, and PTO administrative authorities. Focuses on how new procedures will be applied, what patents are covered, and standards for stays, appeals, and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Program for Business Method Patents (Schumer-Kyl proceeding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporary administrative alternative for reviewing business method patents intended to provide a cheaper, faster substitute for district court litigation over validity of business-method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program authorizes PTO to institute post-grant review of covered business method patents; intended to reduce burden on courts and economy from poor-quality business-method patents. Should be administered appropriately by PTO and courts; designed to be used instead of, rather than in addition to, civil litigation. Has limits on scope, timing, and eligibility (see related criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for instituting post-grant review of business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings will only be instituted upon a high up-front showing of likely invalidity; if PTO determines the patent is a 'covered business method patent' and other requirements are met, the PTO would institute post-grant review and may consider any challenge that could be heard in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proceeding has a higher threshold than current reexamination before the PTO; as a practical matter, a patent without any serious challenge would never be subject to a proceeding. The PTO may consider all challenges that a court could hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional intent on granting stays during business-method proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional intent that a stay of district court litigation in relation to these proceedings should generally be granted and denied only in extremely rare instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment expressly authorizes a stay and places a very heavy thumb on the scale in favor of a stay being granted. If a proceeding is instituted, the district court is expected to stay litigation absent extraordinary circumstances; if a stay is denied, PTO should expedite review (e.g., regulations to complete review in compressed timeframe such as within 6 months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Broadcast Innovation four-factor test for stay motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are instructed to apply the four-factor Broadcast Innovation test when evaluating motions to stay pending PTO proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amendment employs the Broadcast Innovation test because it properly emphasizes the fourth factor—'whether a stay will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and on the court.' By adopting this four-factor test, the amendment precludes courts from inventing additional uncodified factors (e.g., extra-statutory estoppel tests) or de facto fourth factors previously used by some courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeal right to the Federal Circuit for stay decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may file an interlocutory appeal directly with the Federal Circuit as of right; the Federal Circuit may not decline to hear the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing of an interlocutory appeal should result in a stay of district court proceedings pending the appeal. The Federal Circuit can and should review the district court’s decision de novo except in unique circumstances (e.g., subsequent interlocutory appeals in same case). This ensures consistent application of standards and prevents forum shopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business method patent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes 'a method or corresponding apparatus' and is intended to encompass all claim types (method, system, apparatus, GUI, data structure (Lowry), storage-medium (Beauregard), etc.). Patent qualifies regardless of claim type or structure; clever drafting should not avoid PTO review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage extends to any claim that is in substance a business method; form should not trump substance. However, patents for 'technological inventions' are excluded (see technological invention exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological invention exception (out of scope for business-method proceeding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excludes 'patents for technological inventions'—patents whose novelty turns on a technological innovation over the prior art, concerned with a technical problem solved with a technical solution, and which require the claims to state the technical features the inventor desires to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not intended to exclude patents that merely use known technology to accomplish a business process. Mere recitation of computer hardware, networks, software, memory, databases, scanners, display devices, ATMs, point-of-sale devices, or other known technologies does not make a patent a technological invention. Combining known technology to perform data processing operations is not sufficient to invoke the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'financial product or service' and ancillary activities covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment covers not only financial products and services but also the 'practice, administration and management' of a financial product or service; intended to capture ancillary activities related to financial products/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancillary activities include, without limitation, marketing, customer interfaces, Web site management and functionality, transmission or management of data, servicing, underwriting, customer communications, and back office operations (e.g., payment processing, stock clearing). A patent need not recite a specific financial product/service; claims only need be broad enough to cover a financial product/service.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a patent is deemed to 'relate to' a financial product/service
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the requirement, the patent claims must only be broad enough to cover a financial product or service; if a patent claims a general online marketing method that could be applied to marketing a financial product/service, it would be deemed to cover one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent holder alleges a financial product/service infringes its patent, that patent shall be deemed to cover a financial product/service for purposes of the amendment regardless of explicit claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on eligible business-method proceedings under managers' amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: The modified Schumer provision limits the proceeding so that: (1) only defendants/accused infringers may invoke it; (2) prior art is limited to old 102(a) publicly available materials (with limited carryover of old 102(b)-type art); (3) the proceeding may not be used to challenge a patent while it is eligible for a PGR challenge (i.e., an FTF patent during first 9 months after issue); (4) the proceeding is available only for four years; (5) stay decisions are evaluated under Broadcast Innovation; and (6) definition of business-method patent tracks Class 705 limited to data processing relating to a financial product/service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limits were added to accommodate industry and PTO concerns and to narrow the program's reach compared to earlier drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level rationale: impaired prior art availability for business methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Business methods historically lacked readily accessible prior art due to non-patentability before State Street (1998) and lack of documentation in patents/journals, leading to lower patent quality and burden on courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This context justifies a targeted administrative review program to address large numbers of potentially invalid business-method patents issued post-State Street.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review (PGR) window and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishes a new administrative procedure for challenging validity of granted patents within a nine-month post-grant window, providing an early opportunity to improve patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR is limited to First-To-File (FTF) patents (no FTI patents in PGR) and can raise a broader range of issues than IPR. Managers' amendment introduces a 'shoot first' provision: a court must consider a preliminary injunction request without taking a PGR petition or its institution into account if patent owner sues within 3 months of issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review (IPR) conversion and timetable
rubrics_metrics.description: Converts inter partes reexamination into an adjudicative proceeding called inter partes review (IPR), which must be completed within one year of institution (extendable by six months for good cause). Proceedings occur before a panel of three administrative judges with decisions appealable directly to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During first four years after new IPR implementation, Director has discretion to continue old inter partes reexam; old inter partes may be used where only patents and printed publications are at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) role and renaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Renames the Patent Board to the 'Patent Trial and Appeal Board' and clarifies its role in administering the new PGR and IPR proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB will handle adjudicative review panels and related procedural administration; a large number of APJs will need recruitment, training, and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Inventor to File (FTF) regime and grace-period rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Moves the U.S. to a 'First Inventor to File' patent regime and preserves/strengthens the grace period: disclosures by the true inventor (or someone who got info from inventor) less than one year before the application is filed will not be held against their application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the one-year period before filing, an inventor who publishes retains an absolute right to priority if they file within one year; no subsequent disclosures after the inventor's disclosure can be used to defeat their application during that period. The Act also creates an administrative proceeding to ensure the first person to file is the true inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's oath or declaration simplification for assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes it easier for assignees to file and prosecute applications where the inventor is unable or unwilling to sign an oath/declaration or is contractually obligated not to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses practical filing challenges when multiple past/present employees may have contributed to the invention; eases administrative hurdles for corporate filers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages: court gatekeeper role and jury instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: While not changing substantive damages law, Section 4 authorizes courts to act as gatekeepers and provide detailed instructions to juries on the most relevant factors affecting damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to increase predictability in damages by guiding jury consideration of factors that have previously produced inconsistent awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO fee-setting authority and funding reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office authority to set its own fees and sets forth procedures intended to ensure proper funding for PTO operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coupled with Coburn amendment to end fee diversion by creating a revolving fund so PTO has direct access to user fees; aims to prevent diversion of PTO funds to other federal spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-issuance submissions by third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits third parties (typically another innovator) to submit relevant information and make statements explaining their submissions while an application is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expands third-party participation to improve examination quality and bring relevant prior art to examiners' attention earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue rules and codification of transfer standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Codifies the transfer-of-venue standard from In re TS Tech USA Corp ('clearly more convenient' standard) and applies it to patent cases generally; clarifies that venue for litigation against the PTO is the Eastern District of Virginia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers' amendment later strikes codification of TS Tech because it already applies in some circuits; the intent is to address venue concentration complaints (e.g., Eastern District of Texas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination protection against inequitable conduct allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizes a supplemental examination process by which patent holders can correct errors or omissions in past PTO proceedings; if additional info presented does not undermine the original patent determination, earlier omission of that information cannot later be used to allege inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows patentees to present additional information to the Office and gain protection from certain later inequitable-conduct allegations if the new information does not undermine patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-entity status and reduced fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishes a 'microentity' category (truly independent inventors) for which the PTO may make additional fee accommodations beyond current small-entity reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A PTO-approved broadening of microentity status is included to entitle qualifying applicants to reduced fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminates the defense in litigation that an inventor failed to disclose the 'best mode,' while maintaining best mode disclosure as a requirement for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change removes what some consider a subjective and possibly irrelevant litigation defense, though applicants must still disclose best mode during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 14 ends the patentability of tax strategies; managers' amendment clarifies that making tax strategies unpatentable shall not be construed to imply other business methods are patentable or valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes possible clarifying language that does not bar patenting of tax software that is novel as software (i.e., where innovation is in the software)--this language may be adjusted or dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where otherwise provided, the effective date of the Act is 12 months after enactment and applies to all patents issued on or after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific provisions may have different effective dates; check relevant section text for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: APJ recruitment, compensation, and PTO administrative flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO is given greater flexibility in paying and compensating the travel of Administrative Patent Judges (APJs) to recruit, train, and retain the personnel needed to adjudicate PGR and IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change to be funded out of existing funds; recognizes operational needs to staff PTAB for new proceedings.
